chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
title: Claude Hopkins publishes Whaley's 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You'
summary: Whaley says he wrote the number at the Lafayette, handed the score to Claude Hopkins, and it was published by Hopkins, Williams and Joe Davis.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Now what about -- we were talking about Claude Hopkins. You mentioned him.

Claude came by -- I had wrote a number, I'd Do Almost Anything for You -- and it became a big hit, Bill Robinson, Jive Smith, Charlie Parker, they all sang it, and the people would start coming up to it and they'd stop.
Now wait a minute -- who did you say wrote that number?
That' my number. I'll tell you about it.

Claude Hopkins came by the theatre, and said, "Hey, Tom give me that number" -- that was next week, see, and I said, "No, I put it on the shelf, we played it enough." So the producer says, Addison Carey, he's a producer, he said, "Yeah, give it to Claude, and Claude will play it down the Roseland Ballroom".
So me, like a dummy, went out and give him the orchestration. About six months later, 'I'd Do Almost Anything For You', by Claude Hopkins, Bob Williams and Joe Davis. So I saw Claude, and I said ...
Oh, Joey Davis -- the guy that had the ruckus around for years.
Yeah, he was a publisher. Joe Davis.

And I said to Claude -- hey, you know, you took my orchestration and you put your name on it. I said to give me $100 -- and you know, he wouldn't give me nothing. So I said, Aha, it wasn't my number anyway, because I'm working for the theatre, and the theatre pays me for all this music.
